Definition: Articulable knowledge deliberately withheld because of secrecy, confidentiality, competition, hierarchy, or distrust.

Sub-Category Name: Knowledge Conveyed Through Examples or Demonstration
Definition: Knowledge transferred through cases, stories, simulations, examples, pointing, or practical demonstration because a sufficient verbal account has not been provided.

Sub-Category Name: Uncommunicated Knowledge Due to Differing Relevance Judgments
Definition: Knowledge that could be articulated but is not successfully communicated because people notice, prioritize, interpret, or assign importance to different aspects of the same situation. The tacitness arises from mismatched judgments of relevance rather than sensory inability.
A person performs or decides effectively but has not consciously identified, reflected upon, or expressed the knowledge being used.
Competence requiring learned bodily control and coordination during physical work or tool-mediated activity.
A learned capacity to detect meaningful visual, auditory, tactile, spatial, or other sensory differences.

Sub-Category Name: Embodied Posture, Balance, and Spatial Control
Definition: Bodily competence involving posture, balance, orientation, movement, distance, positioning, or spatial awareness.

Sub-Category Name: Immediate Embodied Response to Changing Conditions
Definition: Rapid bodily or neurophysiological response to hazards or changing conditions, often preceding complete conscious reasoning.

Sub-Category Name: Shared Professional Language and Contextual Meaning
Definition: Understanding that depends on participation in a community sharing specialized terms, categories, expressions, narratives, and contextual meanings.

Sub-Category Name: Shared Professional Norms and Standards of Judgment
Definition: Judgment grounded in collectively learned expectations about what is appropriate, acceptable, credible, safe, or legitimate.

Sub-Category Name: Informal Coordination, Communication, and Escalation Know-how
Definition: Unwritten conventions governing coordination, communication, negotiation, signalling, collaboration, contact, and escalation within a group.

Sub-Category Name: Organizational Culture and Unwritten Working Practices
Definition: Knowledge embedded in organizational identity, traditions, routines, authority relations, and historically developed ways of working.
Maps tacit knowledge that cannot be assigned to TK01-TK12 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Articulated and persistently recorded statements specifying what is required, permitted, prohibited, or formally recommended, including laws, regulations, standards, codes, and mandatory thresholds.
Articulated and persistently recorded statements of what is or was the case, including facts, observations, measurements, records, classifications, attributes, and historical descriptions.

Articulated and persistently recorded knowledge explaining how an activity should be performed, including instructions, methods, algorithms, checklists, operating procedures, and prescribed controls; uncodified expert know-how is excluded.
Articulated and persistently recorded accounts of why or how a condition, event, or relationship occurs, including causal mechanisms, interpreted patterns, and reasoned explanations.
Articulated and persistently recorded forecasts, simulations, estimates, or inferential statements about likely future states, consequences, risks, or performance.
Articulated and persistently recorded criteria, instruments, frameworks, scales, protocols, and decision rules specifying how an entity, condition, intervention, or performance should be assessed.
Articulated and persistently recorded results produced through measurement, calculation, assessment, or evaluation, including scores, indicators, KPIs, observed effects, and quantified outcomes.

Lessons or insights from situated experience that have been articulated and persistently recorded, including lessons learned, after-action findings, critical-incident accounts, case reflections, and reusable project insights; experience retained only in a person's mind is excluded.
Maps explicit knowledge that cannot be assigned to EK01-EK08 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Foundational core models, connectionist AI, natural language processing architectures, and generative systems.
User experience design, interactive software interfaces, and spatial computing environments.

Sub-Category Name: Cyber-Physical Systems, IoT, and Smart Environments
Definition: Hardware-software integration where computational logic interacts directly with physical mechanics and automated hardware feedback.
The structural storage, architecture, indexing, retrieval, and semantic mapping of data and structural knowledge.
The hardware, telemetry, and signal/image processing algorithms required to capture and perceive environmental inputs.
Systems designed to ensure data integrity, privacy preservation, confidentiality, and architectural trust.
Network communication protocols, distributed social systems, and mobile-first software application ecosystems.
Deterministic, symbolic, and non-probabilistic AI that drives automated decision-making through hard-coded logic and expert rules.
Maps Digital Technology that cannot be assigned to TE01-TE08 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Observation-based learning in which a learner physically accompanies an experienced practitioner on-site to absorb embodied routines, contextual judgment, and uncodified field maneuvers.
Systematic movement of personnel across operational roles or functions to develop cross-functional mental models, coordination awareness, and holistic understanding of project risks.
Highly structured and targeted physical or mental repetition, including defined self-study protocols, undertaken to master a specific operational proficiency through feedback and correction.
Open, semi-structured conversational forums in which participants exchange perspectives, surface group memory, and collaboratively interpret shared problems.
Structured elicitation sessions designed to extract, decompose, clarify, and document an expert's tacit decision rules, especially for organizational retention or succession.
Retrospective elicitation focused on human behavior, decisions, and causal conditions during a specific significant, exceptional, or hazardous event.
A sustained master-apprentice or expert-novice relationship that transfers contextual know-how, professional judgment, safety norms, and occupational identity through personalized guidance.
Use of oral, written, or facilitated narratives to transmit experiential knowledge, historical lessons, organizational culture, and context-rich understanding.
A timely and structured post-event or post-milestone team debrief that examines what occurred, why it occurred, what was learned, and how future action should change.
A continuing, practitioner-led social network whose members regularly solve shared problems, refine practice, and maintain collective or institutional memory.

Instructor-directed transfer of established knowledge through lectures, presentations, seminars, demonstrations, inductions, or workplace briefings, without the individualized continuity of mentoring.
Human learning or knowledge dissemination primarily mediated by prepared codified materials such as manuals, textbooks, leaflets, instructional videos, photographs, or static presentations.

Learning through direct participation in authentic work, site exposure, applied projects, or practical experience when the evidence does not establish job shadowing, rotation, mentoring, or deliberate repetition.

Facilitated, episodic group exercises, meetings, or workshops in which participants learn jointly, but which lack the open knowledge-café format or the continuing identity and self-organization of a community of practice.
Human preparation, recording, annotation, organization, classification, cross-referencing, or storage of explicit knowledge without automated knowledge-processing support.

Human expert evaluation, checking, consensus formation, prioritization, or iterative refinement of a knowledge product or decision; the principal purpose is validation rather than tacit-knowledge extraction.
Maps Traditional Human-central Practices that cannot be assigned to THR01-THR18 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.

Maps legislation, statutory codes, public policy, government standards, regulatory tariffs, political instability, geopolitical conditions, and jurisdictional requirements imposed by external authorities.
Maps macroeconomic conditions, market fluctuations, industry competition, sector structure, labor-market conditions, workforce demographic shifts, and industry-wide technological change.
Maps societal values, cultural expectations, public attitudes, population demographics, community characteristics, and social norms affecting construction or knowledge practices.
Maps broad climatic patterns, seasonal cycles, extreme weather, temperature regimes, flooding, storms, and other naturally occurring conditions affecting construction activities.

Maps regional or sector-level internet access, communication networks, electricity supply, public utilities, technology availability, and externally provided infrastructure required for construction or digital activities.
Maps requirements imposed by clients, tendering systems, procurement institutions, bid-evaluation criteria, contractual submission conditions, professional bodies, and accreditation institutions.
Maps external suppliers, transportation networks, material availability, delivery dependencies, logistics systems, and interorganizational supply-chain conditions.

Maps the immediate external conditions of a project or workplace, including site geometry, spatial boundaries, congestion, confined spaces, water crossings, terrain, geographic isolation, and structural positioning.

Maps the availability and reliability of electricity, internet connectivity, wireless networks, data transmission, and peripheral infrastructure at the specific site where a technology or KM practice is implemented.

Environmental dependencies arising from the characteristics, circumstances, or eligibility status of intended users that determine whether and how they can access, participate in, or benefit from a technology, programme, training activity, or organizational intervention.
Maps externally originating dependencies that cannot be assigned to ED01–ED09 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Formal policies, mandates, technical standards, protocols, approvals, audits, privacy rules, ethics clearances, and stewardship controls.
Executive commitment, strategic vision, championship, management buy-in, advocacy, and high-level institutional backing for technology-enabled knowledge retention and organizational learning.

Availability and organizational readiness of budgets, facilities, hardware, software, platforms, integrated infrastructure, and usable data. Covers internal technological capacity, but not intrinsic technology properties such as accuracy or reliability.
Protected time, workload allowances, activity duration, delivery sequence, class size, and other scheduling arrangements.
Staff availability, competence, training, facilitation, departmental responsibility, expert participation, stakeholder engagement, retention, mentoring, validation, and succession.

Trust, psychological safety, openness, intrinsic knowledge-sharing motivation, learning orientation, technology receptiveness, and continuous-improvement norms. Also covers negative states such as knowledge hiding, fear, destructive internal competition, and weak learning cultures.

Extrinsic knowledge-sharing motivation through rewards, allowances, recognition, promotion criteria, targets, and performance measures tied to knowledge retention or technology use. Competitive incentives that encourage hiding also belong here.
Hierarchy, organizational maturity, workflow configuration, technology–workflow fit, content or interface design, customization, compatibility, and curriculum alignment not governed by OD01–OD07.
Maps organizational dependencies that cannot be assigned to OD01–OD08 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.

Loss, weakening, or fading of previously acquired knowledge over time. Use only when information was initially learned and later forgotten or retained poorly. Excludes poor initial learning caused by instructional design, which belongs to LI04.

Sub-Category Name: Individual Ergonomic, Usability and Immediate Safety Risks
Definition: Immediate discomfort, fatigue, cybersickness, physical strain, usability burden, withdrawal caused by discomfort, or direct exposure to injury associated with equipment, interfaces, or work settings.

Sub-Category Name: Human Physiological, Cognitive-Capacity and Demographic Constraints
Definition: Relatively stable individual differences or biological constraints, including age-related capability differences, health conditions, sensory or motor limitations, working-memory capacity, and heterogeneous learner characteristics. Excludes temporary discomfort classified under LI02 and acquired-knowledge decay classified under LI01.

Sub-Category Name: Instructional Design, Delivery, Assessment and Transfer Shortcomings
Definition: Weaknesses in training or educational architecture, including passive delivery, inadequate engagement, restricted content, limited instructional methods, poor assessment coverage, insufficient practical access, cognitive overload caused by presentation design, and failure to transfer learning into practice.

Sub-Category Name: Software, Algorithmic, Data Quality and Interoperability Barriers
Definition: Limitations in software functionality, algorithms, model accuracy, computational methods, data completeness or structure, information retrieval, file formats, OCR, language processing, system integration, and cross-platform interoperability. Operational data scarcity belongs here when it constrains a deployed system; research-sample scarcity belongs to LI14.

Sub-Category Name: Hardware, Sensor and Technical Infrastructure Constraints
Definition: Limitations involving physical devices, sensor accuracy or availability, processing capacity, networks, transmission infrastructure, facilities, spatial operating areas, and other physical technical resources. Excludes acquisition cost, which belongs to LI07.

Insufficient funding or excessive acquisition, development, production, licensing, implementation, or maintenance cost. Code time or staffing burdens separately under LI08 when both mechanisms are present.

Sub-Category Name: Time, Staffing, Expertise, Scheduling and Workload Constraints
Definition: Scarcity of time, personnel, specialist expertise, implementation resources, scheduling capacity, or attention; excessive workload; time-intensive development or curation; and delays in realizing benefits.

Sub-Category Name: Organizational Culture, Leadership and Adoption Barriers
Definition: Resistance to change, weak leadership support, authoritarian or abusive leadership, lack of trust or incentives, knowledge hoarding, low motivation, poor participation, group-dynamic problems, reluctance to share, and underuse or rejection of available technologies or practices.

Sub-Category Name: Knowledge Continuity, Documentation, Governance, Privacy and Security
Definition: Failure to capture, preserve, document, retrieve, govern, or transfer organizational knowledge; knowledge loss caused by turnover, retirement, or temporary teams; fragmented documentation; confidentiality, privacy, consent, access-control, and security risks.

Uncontrolled or difficult-to-control physical and operational conditions, including weather, biological deterioration, structural decay, irregular space use, unpredictable occupant behavior, and divergence between planned and actual operating conditions. Human behavior belongs here when treated as external operational variability; deliberate resistance belongs to LI09.

Sub-Category Name: Market, Commercialization, Regulatory and External Institutional Change
Definition: Constraints arising outside the focal organization, including market shifts, commercialization pressure, labor-market change, regulatory change, industry-standard change, and other external institutional developments. Excludes internal culture and managerial choices classified under LI09.

Sub-Category Name: Research Design, Measurement and Validation Flaws
Definition: Weaknesses in the study producing the evidence, including missing controls, inability to isolate causal contributions, narrow measurement instruments, untested outcomes, construct-validity problems, inappropriate comparisons, and insufficient validation. These records are methodological exclusions rather than substantive sector limitations.

Small, narrow, imbalanced, localized, or unrepresentative research samples, including insufficient evaluation or model-training observations when the deficiency arises from the study design. These records are methodological exclusions rather than substantive sector limitations.
Maps limitation that cannot be assigned to LI01–LI14 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Community members who preserve and transmit local, cultural, historical, or intergenerational knowledge.
Practitioners holding embodied, experience-based, manual, or craft knowledge acquired through sustained practice.
Personnel who apply process, safety, service, production, or equipment knowledge in day-to-day operations.
People holding experiential knowledge derived from using a product, service, facility, or system and who communicate that experience.
Professionals holding formal scientific, analytical, design, diagnostic, or technical knowledge.
Recognized specialists who provide expert judgment, validation, evaluation, prioritization, or advisory knowledge.
Managers coordinating people, processes, projects, resources, or operational implementation.
Senior leaders holding enterprise-level strategic, governance, investment, or decision-making knowledge.

Sub-Category Name: Public Authorities, Regulators, and Standard-Setting Bodies
Definition: Actors holding statutory, regulatory, compliance, policy, inspection, or standards knowledge.
Actors who generate knowledge through research, investigation, modelling, analysis, or system development.
Actors who intentionally transfer knowledge through education, training, coaching, facilitation, or mentorship.
Colleagues or peers who demonstrably exchange knowledge through collaboration, mutual assistance, or peer learning.
Actors holding knowledge of markets, customers, procurement, finance, sales, logistics, contracting, or supply networks.
Teams, departments, professional communities, partnerships, or stakeholder networks that collectively hold and exchange knowledge.

Sub-Category Name: Other (*) – Insufficient Evidence of a Knowledge-Holding Role
Definition: Actors whose evidence establishes participation or knowledge receipt but does not demonstrate knowledge possession, application, contribution, or sharing.
Maps knowledge holders that cannot be assigned to KH01-KH15 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Students acquiring domain knowledge through a university course, degree module, or academically situated training activity.
Participants enrolled in a planned vocational, professional-development, induction, or safety-training intervention, regardless of prior occupation.
New, younger, or less-experienced personnel receiving guidance, mentoring, or technology transfer to develop workplace competence.
Established professionals or workers acquiring new technical, digital, safety, or procedural capabilities as part of continuing practice.
Site-level workers who receive hazard, prevention, or protective knowledge intended for direct application in operational safety.
Managers, operators, or other decision users who absorb analyzed knowledge to understand conditions and improve operational choices.
Visitors, tourists, users, or members of the public who acquire cultural or historical knowledge through interpretive, immersive, or participatory experiences.
Members of place-based or indigenous communities who receive, retain, or renew locally embedded cultural and practical knowledge.
Teams, crews, employees, project members, or stakeholder groups that acquire and circulate knowledge as a collective organizational capability.
Expert or research groups that interpret, review, annotate, or validate knowledge artifacts while preparing them for reliable organizational use.
Maps knowledge learner that cannot be assigned to KL01-KL10 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.
Uses BIM, 3D/4D models, engineering simulations, virtual models, and computational scenarios to represent assets, environments, construction processes, system behavior, and performance relationships.

Sub-Category Name: Spatial Knowledge Capture and Geospatial Reconstruction
Definition: Uses UAVs, photogrammetry, laser scanning, GIS, and surveying technologies to convert physical and spatial conditions into measurable digital representations.

Sub-Category Name: Situated Experiential Learning through Extended Reality
Definition: Uses VR, AR, MR, CAVE, or hybrid XR environments to support embodied rehearsal, contextual guidance, historical interpretation, hazard recognition, and situated knowledge transfer.

Sub-Category Name: Interactive Consequence Learning and Digital Feedback
Definition: Uses responsive simulations, animations, indicators, interfaces, or multisensory feedback to make relationships between actions, system states, and consequences experientially perceptible.

Sub-Category Name: Real-time Condition Intelligence through IoT Monitoring
Definition: Uses connected sensors and real-time data streams to capture building performance, occupancy, environmental conditions, and operational states.

Sub-Category Name: Worker Activity and State Capture through Wearable Sensors and Cameras
Definition: Uses IMUs, wearable sensors, eye trackers, cameras, and video analysis to record workers’ movement, posture, gaze, workload, task sequences, and situated work activities.
Uses AI, machine learning, NLP, statistical learning, or rule-based algorithms to derive classifications, forecasts, detected patterns, and predicted conditions from data.

Sub-Category Name: Generative Knowledge Synthesis and Content Production
Definition: Uses generative AI to combine requirements, contextual data, and retrieved knowledge into new drafts, reports, explanations, summaries, or recommendations.
Uses knowledge graphs, semantic metadata, embeddings, vector databases, and meaning-based search to represent knowledge relationships and retrieve contextually relevant information.
Preserves and retrieves codified project records, narratives, lessons learned, safety information, and operational knowledge through databases, data warehouses, or conventional KMS repositories.

Sub-Category Name: Collaborative Knowledge Co-creation through Digital Platforms
Definition: Uses portals, messaging systems, shared virtual environments, and online collaboration platforms to support peer exchange, collective interpretation, user contribution, and shared knowledge construction.
Combines digital content, interactive media, online resources, and face-to-face or workplace activities to strengthen demonstration, participation, and knowledge internalization.
Measures, compares, scores, or ranks learners, models, interventions, and alternatives using predefined criteria, indicators, benchmarks, or performance metrics.
Maps Technology-enable practices that cannot be assigned to TP01-TP13 because the evidence does not identify a sufficiently specific domain or analytical level.

Uses blockchain or distributed-ledger technologies to create verifiable transaction records, strengthen provenance and supply-chain traceability, validate products, and automate trusted exchanges through smart contracts or related mechanisms.

Uses structured games, quizzes, cards, role-playing scenarios, and realistic problem cases to help learners reconstruct procedural sequences, apply operational criteria, recognize errors, and select appropriate responses.
